title: Axiom Releases Open-Source Code for Math's Largest Verified Proof and Fixes Historical Errors
summary:
The makers of AxiomProver have shared the digital translation of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups on GitHub, enabling researchers to validate every logical step of the proof through code. During the formalization process, the startup's AI agents identified 34 discrepancies in the published work, including errors in a 1986 argument for the Unbalanced Group Theorem. To fix the flaw, the system developed an alternative proof based on research from 1976, which allowed the underlying theorem to remain intact while correcting the historical record.

The project utilized a swarm of AI agents to convert roughly 15,000 pages of text authored by more than 100 mathematicians into 43 million lines of Lean code. The $1.6B startup completed the translation in 24 days, a task that involved dividing the work into 380 separate segments and checking the results of 715 different papers and books. The result is the largest computer-verified proof in history, eliminating the need for a human to manually read the entire interconnected body of work to verify its accuracy.

selectedTweets.text:
While formalizing the Classification of Finite Simple Groups, Axiom reports finding counterexamples to an intermediate claim in John Walter’s 1986 argument for the Unbalanced Group Theorem.

The theorem itself survived. AxiomProver developed an alternative argument drawing on Ronald Solomon’s 1976 work, including a new result called “preservation of simple tops.”

Axiom’s mathematicians subsequently found a shorter route to the required conclusion. The accompanying paper records both arguments.

selectedTweets.text:
"We saw a glimpse of the future of swarm coding."

Agent swarms will fundamentally change how we build software.

@axiommathai used a swarm of agents to formally verify the Classification of Finite Simple Groups, the largest proof in math history. That is roughly 15,000 pages by over 100 mathematicians, now about 50 million lines of Lean, verified in 24 days.

The agents claimed tasks, wrote proofs, reviewed each other, and merged their own work through GitHub. Along the way, they fixed hundreds of major errata in the published proof.

selectedTweets.text:
Big win for verifiable AI.

Formal Math proof is starting to scale like software.

@axiommathai rewrote the longest proof in mathematics, all 15,000 pages, about 40 million lines of Lean. 
Swarms of AI agents wrote it in 24 days while mathematicians steered them.

Axiom says that at the start of this year, getting AxiomProver to write a correct 10,000-line Lean proof took weeks of coaxing. And now this swarm of agents formalized a problem roughly 4,000 times that size in 24 days.

The target was the Classification of Finite Simple Groups: about 15,000 pages, 500+ papers, around 100 authors, and no single reader who has gone through all of it.

Axiom credits the jump to rebuilding three layers at once: the models, the harness and the infrastructure.
